cards.title: GNPS Program 9: Professionalism in Nursing Practice
cards.body: Professional Practice and Ethics — Level 2: International Qualified Nurse (IQN)

cards.title: Welcome to GNPS Level 2
cards.body: Nurses entering an international healthcare system must adapt to different legislation, professional standards, regulatory expectations and cultural contexts — while maintaining safe and ethical care.

bullets.label: This level bridges national nursing preparation
bullets.text: This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations, strengthening ethical reasoning, accountability, advocacy, documentation and cultural safety.

bullets.label: Professional accountability remains personal — even within a team.
Interpret local nursing standards and codes of conduct
Distinguish legal, ethical and professional responsibilities
Apply consent, privacy and mandatory-reporting requirements
Delegate and supervise according to scope and patient stability
Advocate for patients across cultural and communication barriers
Document complex care and escalation clearly

cards.title: Your Learning Goal
cards.body: Ethically sound. Culturally safe. Legally responsible.

bullets.label: By completing Level 2, you will be equipped to
bullets.text: By completing Level 2, you will be equipped to provide professional nursing care within international healthcare environments — with confidence and integrity.

bullets.label: Understand local frameworks before practising independently
Navigate complex decisions with a transparent framework
Deliver care that respects every patient's experience
Record care and escalation with precision

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements

bullets.label: Professional regulation differs between
bullets.text: Professional regulation differs between countries, but the underlying expectations are consistent: practise safely, maintain competence, protect the public and comply with lawful standards.

bullets.label: An IQN must understand the local framework
bullets.text: An IQN must understand the local framework before practising independently — orientation and clarification are professional obligations, not signs of weakness.

cards.title: Core Regulatory Concepts
cards.body: Regulatory Frameworks

bullets.label: Nurse practice laws, registration conditions
bullets.text: Nurse practice laws, registration conditions and professional standards define expectations for competence, conduct and accountability.

bullets.label: Codes describe professional behaviour;
bullets.text: Codes describe professional behaviour; standards describe expected practice. Organisational policies provide local processes but do not replace professional judgement.

bullets.label: May include reporting suspected abuse, impaired
bullets.text: May include reporting suspected abuse, impaired practice, serious misconduct or communicable disease. Know your local obligations.

bullets.label: Complete orientation, verify scope and ask for
bullets.text: Complete orientation, verify scope and ask for supervision when systems or requirements are unfamiliar. Seeking clarification is professional practice.

cards.title: Section 1: Clinical Scenario
cards.body: An IQN is uncertain whether a suspected safeguarding concern must be reported directly to an external authority.

bullets.label: The nurse consults the local policy and senior clinician immediately — rather than relying on previous-country practice.
Outcome: The correct reporting pathway is followed safely and on time.

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making

bullets.label: Complex decisions arise when capacity is
bullets.text: Complex decisions arise when capacity is uncertain, family views conflict, treatment burdens are high or urgent action is required. Nurses need a transparent process that separates facts, values, law and professional obligations.

bullets.label: Hold information long enough to decide
Capacity is decision-specific and may fluctuate
Substitute decisions must reflect the person's known wishes, values and best interests
Complex or unresolved conflict may require ethics consultation, legal advice or specialist support

cards.title: Ethical Decision-Making Framework
cards.body: Consider Options

bullets.label: A structured approach ensures every ethical
bullets.text: A structured approach ensures every ethical decision is traceable, defensible and patient-centred. Documentation of the reasoning and consultation trail is essential for accountability.

cards.title: Section 2: Clinical Scenario
cards.body: An older patient with fluctuating delirium refuses a procedure. Capacity may vary throughout the day.

bullets.label: Ensures any decision follows the legal process
Does not assume incapacity without assessment
Document every step of the decision-making process — including who was consulted and when.

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability

bullets.label: International teams include different nursing
bullets.text: International teams include different nursing categories and support roles. Safe delegation requires knowledge of local scopes, patient stability and the competence of the person receiving the task.

cards.title: Delegation and Advocacy in Practice
cards.body: Local Scope and Role Clarity

bullets.label: Titles and responsibilities differ across
bullets.text: Titles and responsibilities differ across systems. Verify role boundaries — never assume equivalence from another country.

bullets.label: Provide direction, monitoring and follow-up proportionate to patient risk and worker competence.
Clarify information, protect vulnerable people, challenge unsafe orders and help patients navigate the system.
Use structured communication and escalation pathways to resolve disagreement without personal attack.

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication

bullets.label: International nurses care for people with
bullets.text: International nurses care for people with diverse languages, values and experiences. Professionalism requires culturally safe communication, protection of information and awareness that power differences can affect participation.

cards.title: Section 4: Key Concepts at a Glance
cards.body: Cultural Safety

bullets.label: Self-awareness, respectful enquiry and attention to how the patient experiences care — not just what is delivered.
Professional interpreters for complex or
bullets.text: Professional interpreters for complex or high-risk discussions. Family may support but cannot replace qualified interpretation.

bullets.label: Electronic records, messaging and remote care require secure access and appropriate information sharing at all times.
Structured handover and closed-loop communication make responsibility and risk visible across disciplines.

cards.title: Program 9 Complete — Well Done
cards.body: By completing GNPS Program 9 — Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to apply international standards, reason through complex ethical issues, delegate safely, advocate effectively and provide culturally safe professional care.

bullets.label: You are now prepared for Level 3 — where the
bullets.text: You are now prepared for Level 3 — where the focus moves to ethical leadership, governance and global professional integrity.

cards.title: Mastering Essential Clinical Skills
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 10

cards.title: Section 1: International Standards & Regulatory Requirements
cards.body: Professional regulation varies across countries — yet the core expectations remain constant: practise safely, maintain competence, protect the public, and comply with lawful standards.

bullets.label: As an Internationally Qualified Nurse (IQN),
bullets.text: As an Internationally Qualified Nurse (IQN), understanding the local regulatory framework is essential before practising independently in any new environment.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Connect local nurse practice laws to everyday professional nursing practice.
Read and apply codes, professional standards, and organisational policy accurately.
Transition confidently into unfamiliar legal and clinical systems.
Recognise the right moment to escalate or consult a senior clinician.

cards.title: Core Concept: Regulatory Frameworks
cards.body: Nurse practice laws, registration conditions, and professional standards collectively define what is expected of every registered nurse — covering competence, conduct, and accountability.

bullets.label: IQNs must proactively research the specific
bullets.text: IQNs must proactively research the specific acts and regulatory bodies governing the jurisdiction in which they are practising.

bullets.label: Ignorance of local law is not a valid defence in professional conduct proceedings.

cards.title: Codes, Standards & Organisational Policy
cards.body: Professional Codes

bullets.label: Describe expected professional behaviour — values, ethics, and relationships with patients and colleagues.
Outline the level of performance expected in specific clinical situations and specialties.
Provides local processes and procedures — supports but does not replace professional judgement.
These three layers work together. When they
bullets.text: These three layers work together. When they appear to conflict, professional judgement and the higher regulatory standard take precedence.

cards.title: Mandatory Reporting Obligations
cards.body: IQNs must understand which events legally require reporting in their country of practice. Common obligations include:

bullets.label: Child, elder, or vulnerable adult safeguarding concerns must be escalated promptly to the appropriate authority.
A colleague whose practice may be impaired by illness, substance use, or other factors poses a patient safety risk.
Certain professional breaches must be reported to the regulatory body, not managed solely within the organisation.
Notifiable diseases must be reported to public health authorities within defined timeframes.

cards.title: Safe Adaptation for IQNs
cards.body: When Systems Are Unfamiliar, Structure Your Approach

bullets.label: Attend all mandatory induction programmes before practising independently.
Confirm what you are registered and insured to do locally — do not assume equivalence.
Ask for support whenever an unfamiliar procedure, system, or requirement arises.
Accurate records protect patients and demonstrate your professional diligence.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Safeguarding Decision
cards.body: "An IQN suspects a potential safeguarding concern. Rather than acting on practice from their home country, they immediately consult the local policy and a senior clinician before taking any action."

bullets.label: This response demonstrates exactly the right
bullets.text: This response demonstrates exactly the right professional instinct — pause, consult, then act — rather than assuming previous-country practice applies.

bullets.label: Check local policy and senior clinician

cards.title: Why This Matters for NCLEX Preparation
cards.body: Safe Care First

bullets.label: NCLEX prioritises questions around safety,
bullets.text: NCLEX prioritises questions around safety, ethical practice, and legal compliance — mirroring real-world regulatory expectations.

bullets.label: Candidates are expected to understand scope of
bullets.text: Candidates are expected to understand scope of practice, mandatory reporting, and patient rights across clinical scenarios.

bullets.label: NCLEX rewards applied clinical judgement — knowing when to act, who to notify, and why policy exists.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Carry these principles into every clinical setting:

bullets.label: Research the specific acts, regulatory bodies, and codes that apply in your country of practice before commencing work.
Policy Supports — It Does Not Replace — Judgement
Organisational policies are guides. Professional accountability remains with you as the registered nurse.
Know exactly what must be reported, to whom, and within what timeframe in your local jurisdiction.
Asking for guidance when uncertain is a mark of competence — not a weakness. It protects patients and protects you.
GNPS Programme 10 · Section 1 Complete. Proceed to Section 2 when ready.

bullets.label: Section 2: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making

cards.title: Why This Section Matters
cards.body: Complex decisions arise when:

bullets.label: A patient's decision-making capacity is uncertain or fluctuating
Family views conflict with patient wishes
Treatment burdens are high or risks are significant
Urgent action is required with no clear directive
Nurses must apply a transparent process that
bullets.text: Nurses must apply a transparent process that separates facts, values, law, and professional obligations — confidently and consistently.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Identify and evaluate factors that affect a patient's decision-making capacity
Use a structured ethical decision-making process in complex clinical scenarios
Facilitate supported or substitute decision-making appropriately and lawfully
Recognise when to escalate unresolved ethical conflict to senior or specialist review

cards.title: Understanding Decision-Making Capacity
cards.body: What Is Capacity?

bullets.label: Capacity is decision-specific — it is not a
bullets.text: Capacity is decision-specific — it is not a blanket status. A patient may have capacity for one decision but not another. It can also fluctuate over time, especially in conditions such as delirium, dementia, or acute illness.

bullets.label: Never assume permanent incapacity without proper assessment at the relevant time.
Hold it long enough to decide

cards.title: Structured Ethical Decision-Making Framework
cards.body: Consider Options

bullets.label: A consistent framework ensures decisions are
bullets.text: A consistent framework ensures decisions are transparent, defensible, and person-centred — protecting both the patient and the nurse.

cards.title: Supported vs. Substitute Decision-Making
cards.body: The Guiding Principle

bullets.label: Support should always come before substitution.
bullets.text: Support should always come before substitution. Explore every reasonable means to enable the patient to make their own decision.

bullets.label: Use plain language and communication aids
Involve trusted persons to assist — not replace
Only appoint a lawful substitute when support is insufficient

cards.title: When to Seek Ethics Consultation
cards.body: Senior Clinical Review

bullets.label: Escalate to a senior clinician when capacity assessment is disputed or clinical complexity is high
Seek legal guidance when decisions may conflict with existing directives, court orders, or guardianship
Refer to a formal ethics consultation for unresolved conflict between stakeholders or care teams
Engage psychiatry, social work, or advocacy services when additional expertise is needed

cards.title: Clinical Example: Fluctuating Delirium
cards.body: The Scenario

bullets.label: An older patient experiencing fluctuating
bullets.text: An older patient experiencing fluctuating delirium refuses a necessary procedure. The nurse must act carefully and lawfully.

bullets.label: Recognises that capacity may vary with lucidity windows
Requests urgent medical assessment during a clearer period
Supports communication using clear, calm language
Ensures any decision follows the legal process — not assumption
Never assume incapacity based on diagnosis alone.

cards.title: Documentation: Your Professional Safeguard
cards.body: Clear, contemporaneous documentation of ethical decisions protects the patient, the team, and the nurse's registration.

bullets.label: Document the time, method, and outcome of any capacity assessment — including who was present
Capture the ethical framework applied, values considered, and options reviewed
Note who was consulted — family, legal, ethics, specialist — and the outcome of each discussion
State what decision was made, by whom, under what authority, and the next steps planned

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.body: Capacity is specific and may change

bullets.label: Always assess at the time of the decision — never assume based on diagnosis or previous assessment
Exhaust all means of supported decision-making before lawful substitution is considered
A structured process ensures decisions are defensible, person-centred, and professionally sound
Record assessment, reasoning, consultations, and decisions clearly and promptly

bullets.label: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional
bullets.text: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability — for Internationally Qualified Nurses preparing for clinical practice and NCLEX success.

cards.title: Section Overview
cards.body: What This Section Covers

bullets.label: International healthcare teams include varied
bullets.text: International healthcare teams include varied nursing categories and support roles. This section equips you with the skills to delegate safely, supervise effectively, and advocate with confidence — all within local regulatory frameworks.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Apply local scope of practice and assess individual competence before assigning tasks.
Monitor delegated care and provide timely follow-up proportionate to patient risk.
Challenge unsafe or discriminatory practices while protecting patient rights.
Use structured communication to resolve professional disagreement constructively.

cards.title: Local Scope and Role Clarity
cards.body: Nursing titles and responsibilities vary significantly across countries and healthcare systems. Never assume equivalence — always verify role boundaries before delegating.

bullets.label: A title used in one country may carry a
bullets.text: A title used in one country may carry a different scope in another. Local frameworks govern what each role may legally perform.

bullets.label: Check registration, competency records, and employer policy — not just job title or assumed equivalence.
The delegating nurse retains professional accountability for the outcome of delegated care.

cards.title: Safe Delegation Framework
cards.body: Assess Task & Stability

bullets.label: Evaluate patient risk and task complexity.
Match competence and scope to the task.
Give explicit steps, expectations, and limits.
Safe delegation is not simply about handing off work. It requires a deliberate assessment of:
Patient stability — Is the patient's condition predictable and low-risk?
Task complexity — Does the task require clinical judgement?
Worker competence — Is the person trained, competent, and within scope?
Complex assessments requiring clinical judgement must never be delegated to workers outside that scope.

cards.title: Supervision of Delegated Care
cards.body: Provide Direction

bullets.label: Give clear, specific instructions. Ensure the delegate understands the task, expected outcomes, and when to escalate.
Proportionate oversight is essential. Higher patient risk and lower competence demand closer, more frequent monitoring.
Debrief after care is completed. Identify gaps, give feedback, and document outcomes appropriately.

cards.title: Advocacy in Clinical Practice
cards.body: Advocacy is a core professional responsibility — not an optional extra. Nurses advocate when systems, policies, or individual decisions threaten patient safety or rights.

bullets.label: Ensure patients and families fully understand diagnoses, procedures, and choices in accessible language.
When an order conflicts with patient safety or evidence-based practice, the nurse has a duty to question and escalate.
Support vulnerable patients — particularly
bullets.text: Support vulnerable patients — particularly those from different cultural or linguistic backgrounds — to access appropriate care.

cards.title: Managing Professional Disagreement
cards.body: Assertive, Not Aggressive

bullets.label: Professional disagreement is addressed through
bullets.text: Professional disagreement is addressed through structure and evidence — never personal attack. Use tools such as SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) to communicate concerns clearly.

bullets.label: State the concern factually and calmly
Support your position with clinical evidence
Escalate to a senior clinician or manager if unresolved
Document all steps taken and decisions made

cards.title: Clinical Example in Action
cards.body: A nurse is asked to delegate a complex clinical assessment to a support worker whose role does not include clinical judgement.

bullets.label: Identifies that the task falls outside the worker's scope of practice.
Communicates clearly and respectfully, without blame.
Ensures the patient is assessed promptly by an appropriately qualified clinician.

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.body: 🔍 Know Every Role

bullets.label: Understand the local scope of practice for every member of your team before delegating.
Assess patient stability and worker skill — both must be appropriate for the task.
Advocacy may require challenging decisions. Do so with evidence, structure, and professionalism.
Unresolved safety concerns must be escalated through formal channels and documented clearly.

cards.title: Mastering Essential Clinical Skills
cards.body: GNPS PROGRAMME 10 · LEVEL 2 · IQN

bullets.label: Section 4: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication

cards.title: Why This Section Matters
cards.body: International nurses care for people with diverse languages, values, and lived experiences. Professionalism demands culturally safe communication, rigorous protection of patient information, and an awareness that power differences can affect how patients participate in their own care.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Provide culturally safe, person-centred professional care
Use professional interpreters appropriately and effectively
Protect confidentiality across digital and verbal channels
Communicate clearly across teams and cultural contexts

cards.title: Cultural Safety in Practice
cards.body: Cultural safety goes beyond awareness — it requires active self-reflection, respectful enquiry, and genuine attention to how the patient experiences care. The nurse's role is to ask rather than assume.

bullets.label: Recognise your own cultural lens and how it shapes your clinical judgements.
Invite patients to share what matters to them — never presume preferences based on appearance or background.
Cultural respect does not lower safety standards; it strengthens therapeutic relationships and clinical outcomes.

cards.title: Communication Access & Interpreter Use
cards.body: When to Use a Professional Interpreter

bullets.label: Professional interpreters must be engaged for
bullets.text: Professional interpreters must be engaged for complex or high-risk discussions — including consent, diagnosis, and discharge planning. Family members may offer comfort and context, but they should never replace qualified interpretation when accuracy or confidentiality is at stake.

bullets.label: NCLEX Principle: Using an untrained family
bullets.text: NCLEX Principle: Using an untrained family member as sole interpreter during consent is a patient safety and ethical concern.

cards.title: Protecting Digital Privacy
cards.body: Electronic records, clinical messaging, email, and telehealth all introduce unique privacy risks. Every nurse is accountable for secure, appropriate information sharing.

bullets.label: Use unique login credentials; never share passwords or leave sessions open.
Share patient information only on a need-to-know basis with authorised team members.
Avoid sending identifiable patient data via unsecured channels or personal devices.
Ensure telehealth environments are private; confirm patient identity before sharing clinical details.

cards.title: Interprofessional Communication
cards.body: Structured Handover

bullets.label: Structured handover frameworks such as ISBAR
bullets.text: Structured handover frameworks such as ISBAR (Identify, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) ensure no critical information is lost at transitions of care.

bullets.label: Closed-loop communication — where the receiver
bullets.text: Closed-loop communication — where the receiver reads back the message — confirms accuracy and assigns clear accountability, reducing preventable error.

cards.title: Clinical Example in Action
cards.body: A patient with limited English is asked to sign a consent form with a relative acting as interpreter. The nurse pauses the process, arranges a professional interpreter, and ensures the patient receives a clear, accurate explanation before making any decision.

bullets.label: Untrained interpreters may omit, simplify, or distort clinical information.
It is always appropriate to pause a procedure until safe conditions are met.
Use teach-back or open questions to verify genuine informed consent.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: 🌏 Cultural Respect

bullets.label: Respecting culture never lowers the standard of care — it elevates it.
Use qualified interpreters for all complex or sensitive clinical discussions.
Protect patient privacy across every communication medium, digital or verbal.
Make responsibility visible and explicit at every transition of care.

cards.title: Practice Safely. Perform Confidently.
cards.body: Section 4 complete — you are one step closer to delivering internationally recognised, culturally safe nursing care.
